title: California utility Permission-to-Operate (PTO) for residential solar/storage routinely exceeds the Rule 21 timeline, stranding installer cash and homeowner tax credits
affected_user: Residential solar/storage installers in PG&E and SCE territory (project managers, interconnection coordinators) and the homeowners whose systems sit installed but un-energized
job_to_be_done: Get an installed system through utility interconnection review to written PTO so the installer can collect final payment and the homeowner can start producing and claim credits
current_process: Installer submits Rule 21 application and post-install paperwork through the utility portal; utility performs engineering review and may require meter swap; written PTO email follows. PG&E publicly states 5-10 business days (max 30 business days) once complete paperwork is received.
what_fails: Installer-reported processing of 4-12 weeks, with full contract-to-PTO cycles of 3-6 months; paperwork rejections and re-submissions restart clocks; at least one CPUC complaint shows PG&E revoking PTO for an installer's systems and substituting a 'Conditional PTO'; a separate CPUC filing shows PG&E paying compensation to a customer for a delayed PTO (settled Dec 15, 2025). Homeowners who finished installs by Dec 31, 2025 but received PTO in 2026 faced uncertainty about 25D credit eligibility.
failure_frequency: unknown at population level; installer blogs describe it as routine in 2025-2026 for SCE/PG&E; CPUC complaint dockets show individual formal complaints reaching settlement
cost_of_failure: Installer final-payment milestones (often 10-30% of contract) deferred weeks to months; homeowner continues paying full utility bill while system idle; possible loss of 25D credit timing (credit ended for systems placed in service after 2025). Dollar totals not found.
existing_workaround: Installers chase utility reps by phone/email, file CPUC informal complaints, keep spreadsheets of pending PTOs; some homeowners file formal CPUC complaints; vendor blogs sell 'faster hookups' as a differentiator
who_pays_today: Installers (working capital, admin headcount), homeowners (idle system, bill), CPUC staff time on complaints

sources.note: PG&E states PTO normally 5-10 business days, max 30 business days, after complete contractor paperwork.
CPUC filing: PG&E agreed Dec 15, 2025 to compensate a customer for delayed PTO on his solar system, settling a complaint.
CPUC complaint describing PG&E revoking PTO for one installer's systems and offering 'Conditional PTO', alleged Rule 21 violation.
Installer blog claims SCE and PG&E are processing applications 4-12 weeks, beyond mandated timelines (vendor source).
Installer guide puts California contract-to-PTO at 3-6 months.
Homeowner asking whether a system finished in 2025 but with PTO delayed into 2026 still qualifies for the federal credit.

firsthand_evidence: A PG&E customer filed a formal CPUC complaint over a delayed PTO and PG&E agreed in December 2025 to pay compensation; another complainant alleged PG&E revoked already-issued PTOs for an installer's customers and downgraded them to 'Conditional PTO'. A homeowner on a tax Q&A site asked whether their PTO slipping into 2026 would cost them the federal credit.
key_unknowns: Actual distribution of PTO wait times across PG&E/SCE/SDG&E in 2026 (no public dataset found); how much of the delay is installer paperwork error vs utility; whether CPUC Rule 21 timeline reporting is public; magnitude of installer working-capital impact.
technical_unlock: Utility portals (PG&E Your Projects, SCE) are web apps that could be monitored with browser automation to surface status changes, flag stalled applications past Rule 21 deadlines, and auto-generate CPUC informal-complaint packets; crowd-sourced PTO-timeline data by utility and circuit would create the missing public statistic.
why_now: NEM 3.0 pushed nearly all new CA installs to solar-plus-storage, which require more complex Rule 21 review; 25D ended for systems placed in service after Dec 31, 2025, making PTO date financially decisive; installer bankruptcies in 2025-2026 shrank the staff available to chase applications.
existing_solutions: Installer-side ops tools (e.g., interconnection tracking features in solar CRMs), CPUC complaint process, no known independent PTO-timeline tracker
verification_status: VERIFIED (delays and formal complaints exist; scale INFERRED)

title: Hundreds of thousands of 'orphaned' residential solar systems have no servicer after the 2024-2026 installer bankruptcy wave
affected_user: Homeowners whose installer (Freedom Forever, Sunnova, SunPower, Titan Solar, PosiGen, ADT Solar, etc.) failed; secondarily local installers/O&M shops asked to take over unknown systems
job_to_be_done: Get a non-producing or faulting system diagnosed and repaired, re-establish monitoring, and enforce equipment and workmanship warranties
current_process: Homeowner calls the defunct installer's number, then the manufacturer; searches for a local installer willing to touch another company's work; takeover installer does a paid inspection, re-links monitoring through the manufacturer portal, and quotes repairs; workmanship warranty is usually gone; leases/PPAs/loans continue with the finance counterparty
what_fails: No system of record maps orphaned systems to willing servicers; homeowners discover production loss months late because monitoring was tied to the installer account; workmanship warranties evaporate; proof-of-claim deadlines in Chapter 7 cases are missed; loan/lease payments continue on dead systems
failure_frequency: One source estimates ~190,000 installed Freedom Forever systems left in limbo after its April 15, 2026 Chapter 11 filing (reportedly converted to Chapter 7 in Aug 2026, unconfirmed); SunPower (Aug 2024), Sunnova and lender Mosaic (Jun 2025), Titan, PosiGen also failed
cost_of_failure: Takeover inspections and repairs are out-of-pocket; lost production while system is down; one source reports rising solar-cancellation requests in California following the Freedom Forever filing; Texas AG opened a consumer-protection investigation (Apr 2026) into Freedom Forever, Sunrun, Lone Star Solar Services and CAM Solar
existing_workaround: Regional installers market 'orphaned solar' service lines; EnergySage and installer blogs publish what-to-do guides; homeowners use the FTC Holder Rule to challenge loans; manufacturers (Enphase, SolarEdge, Tesla) re-assign monitoring on request
who_pays_today: Homeowners (inspection fees, repairs), takeover installers (customer acquisition), manufacturers (warranty labor), state AGs and bankruptcy trustees

sources.note: Installer write-up of Freedom Forever Chapter 11 (Apr 15, 2026), ~2 GW installed across 35 states.
Lists Titan, SunPower, Sunnova, PosiGen, Freedom Forever as failed 2024-2026; notes Texas AG investigation and Chapter 7 proof-of-claim deadline.
Press release reporting rising California cancellation requests after the Freedom Forever filing (self-interested source).
Explains that equipment warranties survive but installer workmanship warranties typically do not.
Example of installers building dedicated 'orphaned solar' service offerings, evidence of a paying market.
Timeline of SunPower, Sunnova/Mosaic, Titan, ADT Solar failures tied to NEM 3.0 and financing costs; cites Wood Mackenzie 21% residential decline forecast for 2026.

firsthand_evidence: No direct homeowner post was retrievable (reddit not fetchable); the pattern is documented through installer service pages describing a steady stream of homeowners calling after their installer vanished, and a press release citing rising cancellation requests in California after Freedom Forever's filing.
key_unknowns: Verified count of orphaned systems and share that are non-producing; whether Freedom Forever is in Chapter 7 or still Chapter 11 (sources conflict); what fraction of homeowners have working monitoring; state AG complaint volumes.
technical_unlock: Bankruptcy dockets (PACER), CSLB license status, and manufacturer monitoring APIs (Enphase, SolarEdge) are accessible to a solo developer; a matching service between orphaned systems and vetted local servicers plus production-anomaly alerts does not require institutional access.
why_now: Freedom Forever's April 2026 filing is the largest residential installer failure to date; 25D ended for 2026, shrinking new-install revenue that used to fund service departments; Wood Mackenzie forecasts a 21% residential decline in 2026, implying more failures.
existing_solutions: EnergySage guides, Solar Insure/ third-party warranty products, regional 'orphan' service installers (ElectriCare, Earthlight, OC Solar), manufacturer support lines
verification_status: VERIFIED (bankruptcies and takeover market exist; 190,000-system figure INFERRED from a single secondary source)

title: Home electrification incentive landscape is churning monthly (25C/25D ended, HEAR/HOMES closing or waitlisted by state), so contractors and homeowners mis-promise, mis-file, and miss rebates
affected_user: HVAC and heat pump contractors, electricians doing panel upgrades, and homeowners in states with HEAR/HOMES programs (CO, CA, GA, CT, OR, etc.)
job_to_be_done: Quote a project with the correct stack of federal, state, and utility incentives, reserve the rebate before install, and submit documentation that is accepted on first pass
current_process: Contractor checks state energy office pages and utility sites, fills state rebate portal forms with income verification, invoices, model numbers and photos; homeowner is told to keep receipts; point-of-sale vs post-install reimbursement varies by state
what_fails: Programs open, pause, waitlist and close within months (Colorado HEAR closed Front Range Apr 28, 2026 and statewide Aug 1, 2026; Georgia paused; California waitlisted; Connecticut not launched); a May 29, 2026 federal notice reportedly stopped HEAR rebates for replacing gas/oil/propane equipment; federal 25C/25D credits ended after 2025. Contractors quote incentives that no longer exist; homeowners lack documentation they didn't know to keep; installers say rebate paperwork is the most frustrating step.
failure_frequency: unknown; multiple contractor blogs in Oct 2026 describe the program status as shifting faster than their own marketing pages
cost_of_failure: HEAR rebates up to $8,000 for a heat pump and $4,000 for a panel upgrade (program maximum $14,000) lost per household when a program closes or paperwork is rejected; contractor sales cycle lengthens; 25C/25D loss alone removed up to $2,000 (heat pump) and 30% (solar/battery) of federal support
existing_workaround: Contractors advise getting the rebate commitment in writing before contract signing; third-party trackers (GridShift, heatpumplocator, energyrebatecalculator) try to maintain state-by-state status pages; some contractors stop advertising rebates altogether
who_pays_today: Contractors (admin time, lost deals), homeowners (lost rebates), state energy offices (program administrators and implementation contractors), rebate-processing vendors

sources.note: Contractor page stating Colorado HEAR closed Front Range Apr 28, 2026 and statewide Aug 1, 2026.
State tracker listing Georgia paused, California waitlisted, Connecticut not launched; cites May 29, 2026 notice ending federal HEAR for fossil-fuel replacements.
Guide on what is left after 25C expired; says forum users consistently name paperwork as the most frustrating step (low-authority).
HVAC contractor confirming no federal heat pump credit in 2026 and listing remaining rebates and a documentation checklist.
Contractor walkthrough of HEAR application steps; advises getting rebate commitment in writing before contract.
Describes HEAR as point-of-sale in some states, conflicting with contractor accounts of heavy documentation, illustrating state-by-state inconsistency.

firsthand_evidence: Contractor blogs (Colorado, Texas, California) say HOMES/HEAR applications require documentation homeowners don't know to keep and that forum users consistently name the paperwork as the most frustrating part; one contractor recommends getting the rebate commitment in writing before signing because programs close mid-pipeline.
key_unknowns: Rejection rates for state HEAR/HOMES applications; number of households on waitlists; whether DOE's May 2026 guidance change is final; how much contractor labor goes to rebate admin per job.
technical_unlock: State program pages, DOE guidance, and utility rebate catalogs are public and scrapeable; Playwright monitoring plus a structured, dated incentive database per ZIP/utility/measure with change alerts is buildable solo; contractors already pay for lead-gen tools that could carry it.
why_now: The 2025 reconciliation law ended 25C/25D after 2025; HEAR/HOMES funds are being exhausted or frozen state by state through 2026; a May 2026 federal notice narrowed HEAR eligibility.
existing_solutions: Rewiring America incentive calculator, EnergySage, GridShift and other status trackers, contractor CRMs with rebate modules, state program implementers
verification_status: VERIFIED (program churn and credit expiration), INFERRED (scale of lost rebates)

title: Green Button Connect utility data APIs are inconsistent or non-functional, so developers and advocates hand-build per-utility scrapers to get interval meter data
affected_user: Developers building home-energy, rate-optimization, VPP and efficiency tools; consumer advocates (Mission:data); Home Assistant users; small energy-service firms needing customer interval data
job_to_be_done: Pull a customer's authorized 15-minute or hourly usage and billing data from their utility in a standard format, reliably and continuously
current_process: Use Green Button Connect My Data OAuth where offered, or Green Button Download XML, or pay an aggregator (UtilityAPI, Arcadia) that itself maintains per-utility connectors and credential-based scrapers
what_fails: Many utility GBC implementations do not meet the Green Button standard; async 'data preparing' 202 responses stall for days; data stops at a date without notice; authorization expires; some utilities' APIs have zero users. Open-source devs maintain a long tail of one-utility integrations (Pacific Power, Con Edison, Consumers Energy, Elexicon, Toronto Hydro) because nothing generic works.
failure_frequency: Per integration, recurring: the HA Green Button issue ran Aug 6 to Oct 25, 2026 across multiple releases before the async problem was resolved and then surfaced a data cutoff at May 6, 2026; UtilityAPI reported Hawaiian Electric's GBC API had zero users as of Jan 1, 2025
cost_of_failure: Developer weeks per utility; aggregator fees; advocacy groups filing testimony; customers unable to use rate-optimization or VPP tools in utilities without working APIs (unquantified)
existing_workaround: Credential-based scraping, manual Green Button XML downloads, paying UtilityAPI/Arcadia, OAuth proxy projects like open-green-button, PUC testimony to force utilities to fix implementations
who_pays_today: Energy-app developers and startups (engineering time, aggregator fees), utilities (compliance), Mission:data and similar nonprofits (regulatory advocacy), hobbyists' time

sources.note: User's Alectra (Ontario) GBC authorization returns HTTP 202 'preparing data asynchronously' for hours; maintainer iterated through 0.2.0-0.3.2 until Oct 25, 2026; returned data then stopped at May 6, 2026.
47 repositories, many single-utility scrapers/importers (Pacific Power, Con Edison, Consumers Energy, Elexicon, Toronto Hydro, PG&E) updated through Nov 2026, showing no generic path works.
Mission:data called LG&E/KU's Green Button Connect 'non-functional' in Dec 2025 testimony; utility disputes it.
Aggregator argues many utility GBC APIs don't meet the standard; Hawaiian Electric's had zero users as of Jan 1, 2025 (vendor source).
Home Assistant community thread on integrating utility data via Green Button Connect.

firsthand_evidence: A Home Assistant user on Alectra Utilities reported that immediately after OAuth authorization the utility returned 'Utility is preparing data asynchronously' and the integration retried every 600 seconds for hours; over the following two and a half months the maintainer shipped several releases, the user then hit 'Authentication Expired', and when data finally imported (about 55,000 readings) it stopped at May 6, 2026 for unknown reasons.
key_unknowns: How many of the ~100+ US utilities with GBC actually work end to end; whether the DOE/NAESB will enforce conformance; what aggregators charge; whether Oregon/CA data-access rulemakings will change this in 2027.
technical_unlock: Open-source OAuth proxy work (open-green-button) shows a stateless bridge is feasible; a public, continuously tested conformance scoreboard per utility, plus community-maintained connectors, is within reach of a solo developer with Playwright and a VPS.
why_now: Rate-optimization, VPP and home-energy tools proliferated in 2025-2026 and all need interval data; CPUC and other PUCs are revisiting data-access rules; Home Assistant Energy adoption raised hobbyist demand.
existing_solutions: UtilityAPI, Arcadia, Bayou Energy, open-green-button, per-utility HA integrations, Mission:data advocacy
verification_status: VERIFIED (failures exist and are recurring), INFERRED (breadth across utilities)

title: Large-load (data center) interconnection queues are swamped by speculative requests, so utilities freeze studies and real projects cannot get a credible power timeline
affected_user: Data center and industrial developers seeking 20-500 MW service; utility transmission planners; ERCOT/PJM staff; state regulators
job_to_be_done: Determine where and when a given load can be served, with a binding cost and date, without waiting years in a queue inflated by duplicate and placeholder requests
current_process: Developer files load-interconnection requests (often the same project at multiple utilities/sites) with minimal entry criteria; utility runs serial or batch studies; ERCOT created a large-load process and 'Batch Zero' study
what_fails: ERCOT's large-load queue grew from ~233 GW (Dec 2025) to 438 GW (Jun 2026) to ~474 GW (Aug 2026), roughly 90% data centers per Gov. Abbott; Texas paused new large-load interconnections and ordered an audit on Aug 3, 2026, delaying Batch Zero; Dominion cannot accept new Northern Virginia large-load requests through 2030; FERC rejected most of PJM's large-load plan. Many utilities lack formal entry criteria, so speculative requests block real ones.
failure_frequency: Queue size tripled in a year at ERCOT (Utility Dive); systemic rather than per-user
cost_of_failure: Per one secondary source, grid delays put ~50% of planned 2026 AI capacity at risk (unverified); utilities respond with study fees, minimum-bill and collateral requirements (AEP Ohio), lengthening timelines for all applicants
existing_workaround: Behind-the-meter gas generation, duplicate filings across utilities, buying existing industrial sites with service, consultants (Keentel, Ascend) to navigate POI studies, state legislation on data center speculation
who_pays_today: Developers (study deposits, consultants, delays), utilities (planning staff), ratepayers (stranded planning), state governments (audits)

sources.note: ERCOT large-load queue at 438 GW when initial process approved.
Texas pauses data center interconnections pending audit; ~474 GW requested; Abbott letter says ~90% are data centers.
ERCOT official says large-load queue grew almost 300% in a year.
Multi-state efforts to curb speculative data center requests; utilities adding fees, collateral, forecast exclusions.
LBNL Queued Up 2026: ~2,061 GW active generation+storage capacity across 8,244 projects, context for the generation-side queue.

firsthand_evidence: Not firsthand from a developer; the Texas governor's Aug 3, 2026 letter (quoted by Utility Dive) states that approximately 90 percent of the new power requests are data centers and demands an audit, and ERCOT responded by delaying its Batch Zero study.
evidence_strength: strong (for the queue statistic); medium (for who bears the cost)
key_unknowns: What fraction of requests are duplicates vs real; average study time per request; whether the Texas audit produces an entry-criteria standard other states adopt; the size of the consultant market.
technical_unlock: Public ERCOT, PJM and utility hosting/large-load data (see github gridprims project built from federal data) could power an independent 'where can N MW actually connect' map; but binding answers still require utility studies, so a solo MVP is informational only.
why_now: AI data center demand surged 2024-2026; FERC Order 2023 addressed generation but not load; Texas SB 6 and the Aug 2026 pause are the first hard brakes.
existing_solutions: Keentel, Ascend Analytics, Enverus/LandGate siting data, utility large-load tariffs, gridprims (open-source)

title: Public EV fast-charger 'uptime' reporting (98-99%) hides a ~71% session-success rate, and new 97% uptime mandates with hourly reporting arrive in 2026 without independent measurement
affected_user: Charge point operators and site hosts receiving NEVI or California incentive funds; fleet operators and drivers who arrive at non-working chargers; state DOTs enforcing 23 CFR 680
job_to_be_done: Prove per-port 97% rolling-12-month uptime to regulators, and actually deliver working charges on the first attempt
current_process: Networks self-report uptime from OCPP heartbeat/availability status; payment failures, vehicle handshake errors and 'live but broken' connectors are not counted as downtime; no third party audits claims
what_fails: ChargerHelp's analysis of 100,000+ sessions on 2,400 US chargers found 98.7-99.9% reported uptime but only 71% of attempts succeeded; NEVI requires >97% per port on a rolling 12-month average; California's rule for incentive-funded DCFC requires 97% average uptime with hourly reporting for six years, starting Sept 28, 2026 per one source (dates vary by source)
failure_frequency: ~29% of charging attempts fail per the ChargerHelp dataset (2025); an April 2026 research citation puts many states' fast-charger reliability at 90-95%, still under 97%
cost_of_failure: Clawback/penalty exposure on NEVI and CA-funded ports; lost revenue per failed session; driver time and stranded fleet vehicles (unquantified in sources)
existing_workaround: CPOs hire maintenance contractors (ChargerHelp, Driivz, Oxmaint-style CMMS); drivers use PlugShare check-ins; third-party aggregators (evchargerscout, ChargeCostLab) compile unaudited rankings
who_pays_today: CPOs and site hosts (O&M contracts, compliance reporting), state DOTs (program oversight), drivers (wasted trips), fleet operators

sources.note: Cites ChargerHelp 2025 report: 98.7-99.9% reported uptime vs 71% session success across 100k sessions / 2,400 chargers; notes no independent auditor.
California Energy Commission document on tracking and improving reliability of the state's EV chargers (primary regulator source).
NEVI 2026 status guide; 97% per-port rolling 12-month uptime requirement under 23 CFR 680.
Vendor page on NEVI compliance maintenance; describes CA 97% uptime rule with hourly reporting for incentive-funded DCFC.
UK comparison: only 3.9% of operators met the 99% rapid-charger mandate per 2025 Monta survey.

firsthand_evidence: No driver or operator post was retrievable; the strongest evidence is ChargerHelp's session-level dataset (via a 2026 secondary report) showing that most charger failures are invisible to network-reported uptime.
key_unknowns: Exact effective date and audit mechanics of the California 97% rule; how state DOTs will verify NEVI uptime; whether session-success data (not just availability) will be required; per-port penalty amounts.
technical_unlock: Open OCPP data, PlugShare-style crowd reports, and public NEVI port lists make an independent uptime/success-rate monitor feasible; a solo dev could build compliance-report generators for small site hosts, but trusted measurement likely needs physical or OCPP access.
why_now: NEVI-funded ports began reporting in 2025-2026; California's hourly-reporting uptime rule starts in late 2026; reliability research in April 2026 shows gaps persist.
existing_solutions: ChargerHelp, Driivz, Paren (reliability analytics), PlugShare, state NEVI dashboards, CMMS vendors
verification_status: VERIFIED (uptime vs success gap), INFERRED (compliance burden size)

title: NYC Local Law 97 compliance paths shift year to year on the Covered Buildings List, and non-filing penalties ($0.50/sq ft/month) often exceed emissions penalties, catching small and mid-size owners
affected_user: Owners and managing agents of NYC buildings over 25,000 sq ft (especially co-ops, condos and small landlords without in-house energy staff); the consultants and registered design professionals who file for them
job_to_be_done: Determine the building's compliance path and filing year, gather 12 months of utility data, and file an accurate LL97 report (and LL84 benchmarking) by May 1 or the grace/extension deadline
current_process: Owner checks DOB Covered Buildings List, hires a consultant or RDP ($), pulls Con Ed/National Grid data, files via DOB BEAM portal; extension available by June 30 for $60, moving deadline to Aug 29, 2026
what_fails: DOB's 2026 CBL memo warns buildings may see a different compliance path than the prior year, and some path changes push the next report to 2027; owners either file unnecessarily or miss a required filing; vendor guides disagree on thresholds; DOB is auditing filings and issuing Notices of Deficiency to non-filers
failure_frequency: One vendor claims ~93% of covered properties filed first reports (unverified), implying thousands of non-filers; path-change confusion is annual
cost_of_failure: Non-filing penalty $0.50 per sq ft per month ($12,500/month on a 25,000 sq ft building); overage penalty $268/tCO2e; false statements up to $500K per violation; consultant fees for filings
existing_workaround: Hire LL97 consultants (Cotocon, Energo, enpg, Insparisk, violationwatch), use NYC Accelerator free advising, file extensions, overfile to be safe
who_pays_today: Building owners (consultants, penalties), DOB (audits), NYC Accelerator (city-funded advising), compliance-software vendors (LLDesk, ViolationWatch)

sources.note: DOB 2026 Covered Buildings List memo: compliance path may differ from prior year; some path changes move the next report to 2027; deadlines confirmed at resolution.
2026 guide: May 1 deadline, 60-day grace to June 30, extension to Aug 29 for $60; penalty figures.
$268/ton overage and $0.50/sq ft/month non-filing penalties; claims non-filing is often costlier than overage.
Vendor claims ~93% first-year filing rate and DOB Notices of Deficiency to non-filers (unverified).
City-funded NYC Accelerator program page, evidence of public spending on compliance help.

firsthand_evidence: No owner post was retrievable; the city's own 2026 CBL memo acknowledges that buildings may find their compliance path changed from the previous year and that for some changes the next report is due in 2027, which is the confusion vendors describe.
key_unknowns: Official non-filing counts and penalties assessed for the 2025 and 2026 cycles; how many buildings had path changes; consultant fee ranges; comparable pain in Boston BERDO, DC BEPS and California AB 802 (not searched due to budget).
technical_unlock: DOB Covered Buildings List, LL84 benchmarking disclosures and BEAM deadlines are public; Green Button/Con Ed data access (see NRG-04) is the hard part; a path-change alert and filing-checklist service for small owners is buildable solo.
why_now: 2024 was the first LL97 compliance year; 2026 is the first year with CBL path changes and DOB audits; penalties for the first cycle are being issued.
existing_solutions: LLDesk, ViolationWatch, Energo, Cotocon, enpg, Insparisk, NYC Accelerator, Bright Power, Measurabl
verification_status: VERIFIED (rules, penalties, path-change memo), INFERRED (number of owners harmed)

title: Residential customers cannot tell which TOU/tiered rate plan is cheapest for them, and utilities rarely auto-correct, so households overpay by the hundreds per year
affected_user: Residential electricity customers in multi-plan utilities (PG&E, SCE, SDG&E, LADWP, Con Edison, PSE&G) and retail-choice markets (Texas); solar and EV owners with unusual load shapes
job_to_be_done: Pick the rate plan (and in Texas, the retailer) that minimizes the annual bill for the household's actual hourly usage, and re-check when usage or rates change
current_process: Read utility rate comparison pages, guess usage patterns, or stay on the default plan; some utilities offer a one-time 'rate comparison' tool; PSE&G offers a 12-month bill-protection credit on its opt-in TOU rate
what_fails: Plans differ in peak windows, tiers, baselines and fixed charges; customers lack hourly data (see NRG-04); Texas retail-choice customers reportedly overpaid ~$4B in 2024 (~$480/household) vs regulated default service (Retail Energy Revealed, Jun 2026, via a retailer); a PG&E bill-review service estimates $180-400/year per mismatched California household (vendor estimate)
failure_frequency: Continuous; every bill until the plan is changed
cost_of_failure: $180-480 per household per year per the above (vendor/advocate figures, unverified); Dallas Morning News watchdog column argues Texas retailers structure plans so customers overpay
existing_workaround: DIY spreadsheets from Green Button downloads, third-party bill-review services, open-source rate optimizers on GitHub (energy-advisor for California, coned-rate-optimizer for Con Edison, SDGE-Analysis), switching to a fixed plan to be safe
who_pays_today: Households (overpayment), bill-review and plan-comparison vendors (affiliate revenue), utilities (customer-service calls), Texas PUC

sources.note: Dallas Morning News watchdog: Texas electricity companies structure plans so customers overpay.
Retailer blog citing Jun 2026 Retail Energy Revealed report: ~$4B / ~$480 per household overpayment in Texas in 2024 (self-interested, unverified).
Bill-review vendor estimates PG&E rate-plan mismatch costs $180-400/year (unverified).
PSE&G TOU is opt-in with a first-12-month bill-protection credit, showing utilities recognize mismatch risk.
Developers building personal rate optimizers (energy-advisor for CA bills, coned-rate-optimizer, SDGE-Analysis) updated Oct-Nov 2026, showing DIY demand.

firsthand_evidence: Individual developers published tools in October-November 2026 that rebuild California utility bills from meter data to find the cheapest rate plan and a client-side Con Edison rate-plan optimizer, indicating people are solving this for themselves because no trusted utility tool does.
key_unknowns: An independent measurement of mismatch overpayment (the $4B and $180-400 figures come from parties selling plans or reviews); what fraction of customers ever change plans; whether CPUC rate-comparison tools are accurate; retailer switching rates in Texas.
technical_unlock: Published tariff sheets plus Green Button interval data allow exact bill re-computation across plans; the blocker is reliable data access (NRG-04), not math.
why_now: Default TOU rollouts in California (2021-2023) and new TOU options in NJ/NY in 2025-2026 multiplied plan choices; rate increases in 2025-2026 raised the stakes; NEM 3.0 export rates depend heavily on plan choice.
existing_solutions: Utility rate-comparison tools, Arcadia, OhmConnect, Texas Power to Choose, My Big Bill, open-source optimizers
